summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman was admitted for acute worsening of chronic lower extremity lymphedema over 2.5 weeks, with significant swelling, weight gain, and discomfort. She was treated with IV furosemide via an existing PICC line, fluid and sodium restriction, and compression. Imaging confirmed no DVT, and her heart function remained stable. The hospital course was complicated by a catheter-associated UTI with Citrobacter freundii, treated with ciprofloxacin. Diuresis was limited by a rise in creatinine to 1.5, prompting transition back to oral bumetanide. Oral thrush and a candidal rash under the breast were treated with nystatin and miconazole. Her INR was optimized to 2.6 on warfarin 9mg daily. She improved clinically, with reduced edema and stable symptoms, and was discharged home on antibiotics, diuretics, and anticoagulation, with strong recommendations to follow up with primary care and a lymphedema clinic.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Infection and inflammatory reaction due to indwelling urinary catheter
Urinary catheterization as the cause of abnormal reaction of patient, or of later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of procedure
Other diuretics causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
